name: Fatima Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential and your name won't be attached. Could you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the ticket-refund queue for a bus operator. A passenger says the machine took a fare twice, and I follow the card record through the till and the bank before we issue a credit. I have a two-year college diploma and I am one of the best on difficult refund cases, though our company pays the leads less than similar work should earn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you work with the screens, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use the AI search now and then, after a colleague has shown me a reliable case, but I still read the actual fare record. My partner Iqbal drives a taxi, and his weeks swing with the weather; our grown daughter has her own bills. We have about three weeks of expenses saved, so I check the next pay date whenever the car needs work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ticket desk that a small shortcut is fine if the fare record still wins an argument. A passenger needs the money returned, not a beautifully phrased explanation of a wrong charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the refund queue to stay busy, and my skill helps with the awkward cases. Iqbal can have a quiet taxi week without warning, and three weeks saved is not enough to make that comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep resolving refunds from the original fare log and ask for the next month's paid rota in writing. In the first year of AI Plateau, Iqbal and I would postpone buying a replacement television while the old one works, and put the avoided cost toward the car-repair reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a bad taxi week, not about this small AI change. A new screen doesn't turn three weeks saved into three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with that double fare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Friday the search summary said a ticket was never tapped, but the fare log showed two taps at the same stop. I gave the passenger the second fare back after checking the bank record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why postpone the television?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old television has a green corner, but it still shows the news. If the taxi needs tyres, a prettier screen in the sitting room will not help us pay for them.

say: I would say the **fare log** still decides a disputed ticket.
I would tell agents a **polished explanation** cannot return a wrong charge.
think: I expect my **refund work** to continue in a mild change.
I worry **Iqbal's taxi weeks** and three weeks saved leave us exposed.
do: Keep resolving **double-fare refunds** against original fare and bank records.
Postpone the **replacement television** and direct that spending to the car-repair reserve.
feel: I feel **anxious** about household income despite steady refund work.
S0.quote: A passenger needs the money returned, not a beautifully phrased explanation of a wrong charge.
fieldNote: Her **high refund skill** supports current work, while household income remains variable.
She delays a **television purchase** to protect money for possible car repairs during a quiet taxi week.

steps.text: Keep resolving refund calls against the original fare and bank records
Postpone buying a replacement television while the current one works
Put the avoided television cost toward the car-repair reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the queue that routine fare questions will move to software, and it had better leave us paid time for wrong charges. I would ask the supervisor for the paid dispute rota before applauding the new checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep the hard refunds, but the team can be smaller and my lead hours could fall. With Iqbal's uneven fares, we cannot treat my title as protection for our weekly bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would learn the new AI fare checker on a paid shift by running fifteen closed double-charge cases, if my supervisor permits error logging. In the first year routine tickets move, I would keep taking paid disputes and ask for the written weekly rota; if its hours fell, I would compare advertised local service desks by full weekly pay and bus cost before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but interested in whether the checker finds the right fare. I would not test live passenger accounts to prove a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fifteen-case test record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record how often the checker misses a second tap and how often the passenger calls again. A quick refund is only quick if we do not make the same passenger ring twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply at the energy desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local energy desk has an advert sometimes, but I have not seen a paid opening this week. I would apply only for a posted role whose written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after my bus fare, and keep my current paid calls until a real offer exists.

say: I would ask for **paid dispute hours** before praising the checker.
I would say **repeat refund calls** matter more than a quick first answer.
think: I may keep **difficult refunds** while losing lead hours.
I cannot treat my **title** as a substitute for weekly pay.
do: Test **fifteen old double-charge cases** with the new AI checker on paid time if approved.
Keep **paid disputes** and request written hours; if they fall, apply only for posted after-bus-fare bill-covering weekly work.
Keep **current paid calls** until a real posted offer exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller paid week, but curious about the checker.
S1.quote: A quick refund is only quick if we do not make the same passenger ring twice.
fieldNote: She tests a **new AI tool** on closed cases only with paid time and error-logging permission.
The fallback requires a **posted paid role** with written full-week wages and hours after bus fare.

steps.text: Test fifteen closed double-fare cases with AI checker on paid time if logging is approved
Keep paid ticket disputes and ask for written weekly hours when routine tickets move
After hours fall, apply for posted paid work with written after-bus-fare wages and hours covering bills
Keep current paid disputes until a real posted offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team full thinking AI by 2028 can decide fare disputes faster than we do, while capable robots for hands-on station work arrive around 2031. That is a direct threat to our desks, not a reason to guess about drivers' jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my paid lead hours could end before another local desk opens. Three weeks saved and Iqbal's uncertain taxi income would not carry the household through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the operator for written notice and the last date of paid dispute shifts, then list bills with Iqbal. If most of my hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid station-counter work only if its written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel; I would keep any paid disputes still offered while asking the landlord for a payment schedule only if rent is actually missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing most of my wage while the car and rent keep needing money. A good refund record will not buy a vacant desk by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the station counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the station counter includes paid passenger-help hours or only an online volunteer scheme. A notice with no weekly pay on it is not an offer I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your daughter help with the search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter could drive me to one interview if her day off lined up, but I would ask her first. I would not write her wages or transport into our plan as though she had promised either.

say: I would warn **2028 thinking AI** reaches fare decisions before 2031 station robots.
I would ask for **written notice** and dates of paid dispute shifts.
think: I expect **most lead hours** could end quickly.
I cannot live through a **long search** on three weeks saved and irregular taxi income.
do: Get **written notice dates** and list bills with Iqbal in 2026.
If most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted paid station work only with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.
Ask landlord for a **payment schedule** only if most hours end and rent is actually missed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a likely large wage loss and current rent.
S2.quote: A notice with no weekly pay on it is not an offer I can use.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** does not create a local paid vacancy after rapid AGI.
She keeps family **transport help** conditional on her daughter's availability and agreement.

steps.text: Keep any paid ticket disputes and request written final paid-shift dates
After most hours end, check posted paid station work's written weekly wages, hours and travel
Apply only if after-travel pay and hours cover bills
If most hours end and rent is missed, ask landlord for payment schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to see if the new checker really reduces wrong fares, not just call numbers. Thinking AI can take refund decisions by 2031; robots reach hands-on station work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep the difficult appeals while standard refunds vanish, but no one has promised my paid lead hours. I would like to see my household's actual income before deciding whether we can reduce work at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep a monthly count of reopened double-fare cases and ask the manager for paid appeal hours beside it. If the checker proves accurate on old cases and my supervisor agrees to paid training time, I would learn its appeal controls; if my own hours fall in the first year after 2031, I would inspect posted local counter roles and their written weekly wages, hours and travel cost before deciding whether to apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours. I can plan and still lose hours. The extra years let me ask whether the tool is accurate before I put a passenger's refund in its hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the checker improved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the same old cases again after each update, so I know if an error really disappeared. I would not call using the same search box 'training' unless I had learned the appeal controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you cut hours at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Iqbal and I would check actual income statements, not guess that the taxi will always bring the same amount. Our daughter has her own bills, and I will not name a pension figure I have not seen.

say: I would ask for **paid appeal hours** beside reopened-case counts.
I would say **2031 refund AI** comes before 2034 station robots.
think: I could keep **hard appeals** without keeping the same paid week.
I cannot assume **later-life income** from variable taxi fares or an unchecked pension.
do: Count **reopened double fares** monthly, retest the same closed cases after each update, and request paid appeal hours.
Learn **AI appeal controls** only if old cases prove accurate and paid training time is agreed.
Inspect **posted counter work** if my hours fall after 2031, checking written wages, hours and travel cost.
feel: I feel **anxious** about hours despite time to test the checker.
S3.quote: I can plan and still lose hours.
fieldNote: Her conditional **new AI learning** differs from existing occasional search use.
A counter enquiry follows an **actual hours cut**, with written wages, hours and travel cost inspected.

steps.text: Count reopened double fares monthly; retest same cases after each update and request paid appeal hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family that a decade can be useful if we keep checking paid work and actual bills, not just the calendar. Full thinking AI reaches ticket decisions by 2036 and hands-on station robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need wages, even if I have led the refund row for years. Three weeks saved does not tell me what income would replace my job or Iqbal's taxi work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Iqbal and I would put our income statements beside a year's bills and check how much of my lead wage pays rent. I would keep handling paid appeals and ask each year for the written dispute rota; after 2036 I would reduce hours only if verified income covers our bills, otherwise I would keep the paid work actually available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's short reserve, with some relief that ten years gives us time to count properly. I will not put a guessed pension on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count taxi income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would list the taxi income by month instead of using its best week. A strong summer does not pay for a quiet winter twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter contribute later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can visit and make tea while we do the figures, but she pays her own bills. I would only include help if she actually offered it and could afford it.

say: I would use the **decade** to check paid work and real household bills.
I would explain **2036 ticket AI** arrives before 2039 station robots.
think: I may still **need wages at 68** despite years as a lead.
I cannot infer **replacement income** from three weeks saved or a guessed pension.
do: Compare **wage statements** and monthly taxi income against a year of rent and bills.
Keep **paid appeals** and request the annual written dispute rota; reduce hours only when verified income covers bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current savings, though time allows a careful calculation.
S4.quote: A strong summer does not pay for a quiet winter twice.
fieldNote: She separates **seasonal taxi takings** from a dependable replacement wage.
She checks **verified income** before reducing paid work or assuming adult-child help that was never offered.

steps.text: Keep paid ticket appeals and request the written human dispute rota each year
Compare wage statements and monthly taxi income with annual rent and bills before reducing work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 one, because my lead work could end before I can find another paid counter. Written hours, a real posted role and time to speak with Iqbal about the bills would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can correct a wrong refund once the software says the ticket is closed. The passenger will still ring somebody when the money is missing.

headlineQuote: The passenger will still ring somebody when the money is missing.
portrait: A **58-year-old** ticket-refund lead with a two-year college diploma and high skill but low pay.
She uses **AI sometimes**, after proven examples, and checks original fare and bank records.
Iqbal's **variable taxi income** and three weeks saved leave little room for a lost lead shift.
She tests **new appeal controls** only with paid time and conditions, while checking verified later-life income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most paid lead hours before another local opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written hours**, a posted paid role and time to compare bills with Iqbal would help.
